Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "we need a clear repair note for the crew at cedar bend orchard, because the east apple block is losing pressure and the morning irrigation has to be planned around the repair. on tuesday, october 14, mara noticed water pushing up through gravel beside valve box E-7, near the service lane. the gauge at the filter house showed 38 psi while zone 4 was running, compared with the usual 52 to 55 psi. rows 18 through 24 were wet near the trunks, but the ground on the downhill side was dry, so the crew has not confirmed how far the leak extends. nobody saw water coming from the valve box itself. the suspected break is in the buried two-inch polyethylene main between E-7 and the first tee, not in a tree-row lateral, but that is still an estimate until the pipe is exposed.

mara and luis shut zone 4 off at 9:20 a.m. and left the other three east-block zones operating. that choice is important because those zones share the filter house but do not use this section of main. they marked the wet patch with two stakes, took a photograph from the service lane, and wrote down the pressure reading before shutting the valve. the crew should not open zone 4 again just to see whether the pressure comes back; reopening it before the repair could send water into the excavation area. the plan is to keep that zone isolated while they dig, and to keep the rest of the block on its normal schedule unless the filter-house gauge falls below 45 psi. if it does fall below 45, pause the other east-block zones too and tell mara before changing their schedule.

there is room to place the excavated soil on the lane side of E-7, but not on the grass strip beside the drainage swale. luis measured about six feet from the valve box to the nearest tree guard, and the pipe route should run under that open strip. the crew has to uncover the line by hand for the first two feet on each side of the suspected break, since a buried electric cable is marked near the lane and its exact depth is not shown on the orchard map. the cable marker is orange and sits roughly four feet west of the wet patch. no one should move that marker or use the excavator inside the marked area. the small excavator can remove soil farther from the cable after luis confirms its location, but the final material around the pipe should be cleared with hand tools so the crew can see the fittings before cutting anything.

mara has set aside an eighteen-foot coil of two-inch polyethylene pipe, two compression couplings, a replacement shutoff valve, and a roll of blue warning tape. the old pipe may only need a coupling, so the crew should not cut out a longer section unless the exposed wall is split or deformed beyond the wet joint. luis said, “the fitting could be the whole problem, but we should look at the pipe before we decide.” the crew also needs to check whether the shutoff valve can close fully; if it does not, they must keep the upstream supply off at the filter-house manifold while the fitting is removed. the valve was stiff during the first attempt, but it did close, and no one has tested it again under pressure. use the replacement valve only if the old one fails that check, not simply because the replacement is already on site.

once the pipe is exposed, the repair sequence should be as follows:
1. confirm that zone 4 remains isolated and note whether the excavation is still receiving water.
2. check the valve and inspect the pipe and both sides of the wet joint before cutting. photograph the exposed connection beside a ruler for the maintenance record.
3. if the pipe wall is sound and only the compression coupling is leaking, replace that coupling and retain the existing pipe. if the wall is split or deformed beyond the joint, remove the damaged section and use the prepared pipe and two couplings; keep the replacement as short as the damage allows.
4. restore the supply slowly and pressure-test the repaired section for twenty minutes while zone 4 stays closed downstream. if the pressure holds for the full twenty minutes with no visible seepage, reconnect the existing lateral at the first tee and reopen zone 4 gradually. if the pressure drops or water appears at the repair, keep zone 4 isolated, expose the next joint on the same main, and replace the damaged coupling before reconnecting the lateral. do not treat a short period without visible water as a passing test.
5. record the final gauge reading, the parts used, and whether the crew followed the coupling-only or pipe-section branch. leave the valve box accessible until mara has reviewed the note.

the first irrigation window for zone 4 is listed for 3:30 p.m., but the schedule should remain tentative until the pressure test is complete. if the repair has not passed the full test by 3:00 p.m., leave zone 4 off for that window and notify mara; do not shorten the test to fit the schedule. if it passes earlier, the crew can reopen the zone gradually after the test and tell the irrigators the actual restart time. the other east-block zones can continue only while the filter-house gauge stays at or above 45 psi, as noted above. the orchard manager needs the record before the next morning's route is assigned, so include the time the test began and ended rather than only writing “passed.”

after the repair, put the excavated soil back without covering the compression fittings until the pressure check and photographs are finished, then place the blue warning tape above the repaired main before the final soil layer is added. keep the soil off the grass strip and leave the orange cable marker in place. if the ground is still saturated when the crew returns the next morning, leave the surface open around the repair and inspect it for renewed seepage before running zone 4; if the ground is no longer saturated, the crew can finish grading the lane-side patch after checking the exposed area once more. in either case, note the surface condition and any water seen at the repair in the same maintenance entry, so the morning crew can distinguish drainage from a renewed leak.", "output": "We need a clear repair note for the crew at Cedar Bend Orchard because the east apple block is losing pressure, and the morning irrigation must be planned around the repair. On Tuesday, October 14, Mara noticed water pushing up through the gravel beside valve box E-7, near the service lane. The gauge at the filter house showed 38 psi while zone 4 was running, compared with the usual 52 to 55 psi. Rows 18 through 24 were wet near the trunks, but the ground on the downhill side was dry, so the crew has not confirmed how far the leak extends. No one saw water coming from the valve box itself. The suspected break is in the buried two-inch polyethylene main between E-7 and the first tee, not in a tree-row lateral, but that remains an estimate until the pipe is exposed.

Mara and Luis shut off zone 4 at 9:20 a.m. and left the other three east-block zones operating. This is important because those zones share the filter house but do not use this section of main. They marked the wet patch with two stakes, took a photograph from the service lane, and recorded the pressure reading before shutting the valve. The crew should not reopen zone 4 just to see whether the pressure returns; doing so before the repair could send water into the excavation area. The plan is to keep that zone isolated while digging and to keep the rest of the block on its normal schedule unless the filter-house gauge falls below 45 psi. If it does, pause the other east-block zones as well and tell Mara before changing their schedule.

There is room to place the excavated soil on the lane side of E-7, but not on the grass strip beside the drainage swale. Luis measured about six feet from the valve box to the nearest tree guard, and the pipe route should run under that open strip. The crew must uncover the line by hand for the first two feet on each side of the suspected break because a buried electric cable is marked near the lane, and its exact depth is not shown on the orchard map. The orange cable marker sits roughly four feet west of the wet patch. No one should move it or use the excavator inside the marked area. The small excavator can remove soil farther from the cable after Luis confirms its location, but the crew should clear the final material around the pipe with hand tools so the fittings are visible before anything is cut.

Mara has set aside an eighteen-foot coil of two-inch polyethylene pipe, two compression couplings, a replacement shutoff valve, and a roll of blue warning tape. The old pipe may need only a coupling, so the crew should not cut out a longer section unless the exposed wall is split or deformed beyond the wet joint. Luis said, “the fitting could be the whole problem, but we should look at the pipe before we decide.” The crew also needs to check whether the shutoff valve closes fully. If it does not, they must turn off the upstream supply at the filter-house manifold while removing the fitting. The valve was stiff during the first attempt, but it did close, and no one has tested it again under pressure. Use the replacement valve only if the old one fails that check, not simply because the replacement is already on site.

Once the pipe is exposed, follow this repair sequence:
1. Confirm that zone 4 remains isolated and note whether water is still entering the excavation.
2. Check the valve and inspect the pipe and both sides of the wet joint before cutting. Photograph the exposed connection beside a ruler for the maintenance record.
3. If the pipe wall is sound and only the compression coupling is leaking, replace that coupling and retain the existing pipe. If the wall is split or deformed beyond the joint, remove the damaged section and use the prepared pipe and two couplings. Keep the replacement as short as the damage allows.
4. Restore the supply slowly and pressure-test the repaired section for twenty minutes while zone 4 remains closed downstream. If the pressure holds for the full twenty minutes with no visible seepage, reconnect the existing lateral at the first tee and reopen zone 4 gradually. If the pressure drops or water appears at the repair, keep zone 4 isolated, expose the next joint on the same main, and replace the damaged coupling before reconnecting the lateral. Do not count a short period without visible water as a passing test.
5. Record the final gauge reading, the parts used, and whether the crew followed the coupling-only or pipe-section branch. Leave the valve box accessible until Mara has reviewed the note.

Zone 4’s first irrigation window is listed for 3:30 p.m., but the schedule should remain tentative until the pressure test is complete. If the repair has not passed the full test by 3:00 p.m., leave zone 4 off for that window and notify Mara; do not shorten the test to fit the schedule. If it passes earlier, the crew can reopen the zone gradually after the test and tell the irrigators the actual restart time. The other east-block zones can continue only while the filter-house gauge remains at or above 45 psi, as noted above. The orchard manager needs the record before assigning the next morning’s route, so include the time the test began and ended rather than writing only “passed.”

After the repair, put the excavated soil back without covering the compression fittings until the pressure check and photographs are finished. Then place the blue warning tape above the repaired main before adding the final soil layer. Keep the soil off the grass strip and leave the orange cable marker in place. If the ground is still saturated when the crew returns the next morning, leave the surface open around the repair and inspect it for renewed seepage before running zone 4. If the ground is no longer saturated, the crew can finish grading the lane-side patch after checking the exposed area once more. In either case, note the surface condition and any water seen at the repair in the same maintenance entry so the morning crew can distinguish drainage from a renewed leak."}]
